newsitem.title: UK: N.Irish Protestants angry after two hurt by bomb.
newsitem.headline: N.Irish Protestants angry after two hurt by bomb.

text.p: Angry Protestant leaders called for tough British sanctions against Sinn Fein, the IRA's political arm, on Friday after a Northern Ireland policeman and a soldier were badly hurt in a guerrilla ambush.
Peter Robinson, the Democratic Unionist Party's deputy chief, called for Sinn Fein to be outlawed and said a government ban on broadcast interviews with its leaders should be re-imposed.

"We really have reached the stage where the government must show the community's disapproval by either proscribing Sinn Fein or making it clear that they are not part of the democratic process. We must return to the situation where we have an effective media ban," he said on BBC radio.

Guerrillas set off a bomb late on Thursday in east Belfast, the second suspected IRA attack in 12 hours. The IRA have been waging a violent campaign for 25 years to oust British forces from the province.

"One police officer and one soldier are being treated for shrapnel injuries," a police spokesman said. "They are seriously injured but (the wounds) are not thought to be life threatening. Four other soldiers were treated for shock."

The explosion happened shortly after British Prime Minister John Major and his Irish counterpart John Bruton had telephone talks about how to unfreeze deadlocked peace efforts, suspended last week until after the British election.
Officials in London and Dublin said their leaders' 25-minute discussions -- their first for several weeks -- were constructive.

Sir John Wheeler, Britain's security minister for Northern Ireland, said the IRA had demonstrated contempt for life and democracy. "They still believe that they can defeat democracy with the bomb and the bullet," he said in a statement.
Reg Empey, a leading negotiator in the Protestant Ulster Unionist Party, said participants in the peace talks should forge ahead with constructing a political settlement and leave Sinn Fein behind.

Sinn Fein is banned from the talks until the IRA reinstates a ceasefire broken 13 months ago with bombs in London. The talks were clouded by a spate of IRA attacks and dogged by inter-party wrangling. The IRA has killed two soldiers since last October.
Empey said the IRA was trying to foment a backlash by pro-British Loyalist guerrillas who are holding to an unstable 29-month truce in a war against Catholic nationalists.

Empey said that the Republican Movement, comprising the IRA and Sinn Fein, were "dabbling in politics on the one hand and dabbling in terrorism on the other." "There has to be a decision taken by government and by others that these people are irredeemable as far as the political process is concerned," Empey told BBC radio.
The six-year ban on the voices of Sinn Fein leaders being heard on British media broadcasts was lifted in September 1994.
